name: Fortress
description: Fortress is a challenging open-information Solitaire (Patience) game characterized by its unique building rules and lack of a draw pile. Unlike many other solitaires, Fortress allows players to build sequences both up and down within the tableau, provided they follow suit. All cards are dealt at the start; the top card of each column is available. Empty tableau spaces may be filled with any available card. It is often cited as a game of skill rather than luck, where planning several moves ahead is essential for victory.

history.origins: Fortress, also known as 'Chessboard' in some regional histories, is an old European solitaire that likely predates the 20th century. Its name is derived from the appearance of the ten columns of cards, which resemble the battlements of a castle's fortress.
timeline: 1800s: Early versions of suit-based building solitaires appearing in France and Germany.
1910s: Formalized in English 'Patience' books as 'The Fortress'.
Present: A standard inclusion in digital solitaire collections for its unique 'two-way building' mechanic.
history.cultural: Regarded as a 'thinker's solitaire' due to the complete lack of hidden information.
history.evolution: The game is a cousin of 'Beleaguered Castle', but differentiates itself by allowing both ascending and descending sequences in the columns.

setup.players: One player only. Fortress is a patience (solitaire) game; the entire deck is laid out at the start and the single player moves cards between the tableau columns and the four foundations.
setup.dealing: Deal 52 cards face-up into 10 columns: two columns of 6 cards (one on the left, one on the right) and eight columns of 5 cards. Four foundation spaces in the centre for aces.

rules.objective: Move all 52 cards into the four foundation piles, building each suit up from Ace to King.
rules.gameplay: Only the top card of each tableau column is available. Move a card to a foundation (build up by suit from ace to king) or to another tableau column (build up or down by same suit, one card at a time; no round-the-corner). Fill an empty tableau space with any available card. No redeal.
keyRules: Only the exposed (top) card of each column is available.
Foundations build up by suit from ace to king.
Tableau builds up or down by same suit; one card at a time.
Aces cannot be placed on kings or vice versa.
Empty spaces may be filled with any available card.

strategy.basic: Prioritize exposing the Aces. If an Ace is buried at the bottom of a 6-card column, you must calculate exactly how many moves it will take to move the 5 cards on top of it without losing access to those cards.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Two-Way Loop': Use the ability to build up and down to shuffle cards between columns. If you have a 4 of Hearts and a 6 of Hearts in different piles, and the 5 of Hearts is available, you can use the 5 to bridge the gap and move segments of the suit together.
strategy.advanced: Conserve Spaces: Do not empty a column unless you have a definitive path to victory. Empty spaces can be filled with any card, but losing a column still reduces maneuverability; use spaces wisely.
tips: Look for 'blocked suits'. If the King of Clubs is on top of the Ace of Clubs, that suit is effectively frozen until you can move the King to another pile.
Always prioritize moves to the foundation over moves within the tableau, unless a tableau move helps unbury a hidden Ace.

variations.name: Chessboard
variations.description: Played like Fortress except the player may freely choose the starting rank of all four foundations. Building can go round-the-corner (aces may be placed on kings and vice versa).
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Chessboard allows free choice of foundation start rank and round-the-corner building; overrides not yet mapped to engine constants.
